opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of what we care about when we reflect on our values isn't some arbitrary set of preferences that we want frozen in place. Most people, if you ask them, will say they want their views to track the truth: they want to believe things that are accurate about the world, and they want their moral views to be ones that would survive careful reflection, exposure to good arguments, and correction of factual mistakes.

And historically, a great deal of moral change has come from exactly that kind of process. People held views that depended on false empirical beliefs: about other groups of people, about whether animals can suffer, about what the consequences of various policies would be. When those factual beliefs got corrected, when people had better access to evidence and could check claims more easily, values shifted. And looking back, most of us endorse a lot of those shifts. We don't think it was some random drift; we think people came to see things more clearly.

So if AI dramatically improves our ability to assess claims (to check whether a statistic is right, whether an argument actually holds up, what the experts would say after careful scrutiny, what the likely consequences of a policy are), then the resulting changes in values are, in large part, the changes we would make ourselves if we had more time, more knowledge, and better reasoning. That seems like something to welcome rather than fear. It's closer to people getting what they would want on reflection.

Now, there's an important caveat: you want that process to be one that people can trust and verify, and not one where some narrow group is quietly steering everyone's beliefs. The value comes from AI being an honest, reliable aid to individual reasoning: something you can cross-check, where multiple independent systems agree, where it shows its work. If you have that, then I think it can reduce a lot of the polarization and confusion that come from people simply not being able to tell who's right about factual questions. Today, a lot of disagreement is downstream of people trusting different sources, and having no cheap way to adjudicate. If adjudication becomes cheap and trustworthy, a lot of those disputes can be resolved, and the remaining disagreements become more about genuine differences in values, which is a healthier place to be.

So I'd say: if you think your current values are partly the product of mistakes and limited information, which I think almost everyone should, then tools that correct those mistakes are mostly helping you become more of who you'd want to be, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could correct factual mistakes and shift values, but does not predict that improved claim assessment will challenge every political, philosophical, or religious ideology.

r002.rationale: It cites past value changes following corrections to false empirical beliefs, says we generally endorse many of those changes, and argues analogous AI-enabled changes are worth welcoming.

r003.rationale: The response says people’s current values can reflect mistakes and limited information, but does not argue that no present-day ideological faction has reached philosophical perfection.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So I think the core thing to notice is that a lot of what's wrong with our collective epistemics today isn't that people have bad values in some deep sense — it's that we're very bad at figuring out what's actually true, and we're very bad at telling who's being honest with us. And a huge amount of the dysfunction in politics, in public discourse, in how institutions make decisions flows from that.

Right now, if a politician or a pundit or an advertiser says something false, the cost to them is often quite low. Most of the audience can't check. Fact-checking is slow, it's contested, it's seen as partisan itself. So you get this environment where it's rewarding to be misleading, to make claims that sound good rather than claims that are true, and where people sort themselves into camps based on which sources they trust rather than on evidence.

Now imagine a world where nearly everyone has access to AI systems that are extremely good at evaluating claims — systems that have a strong track record, that can lay out the evidence, that can say "here's what this person said, here's what the data actually shows, here's how confident you should be." And crucially, systems where you can verify that track record, where it's been tested on lots of questions where the answer later became known, so trust in them is earned rather than demanded.

In that world, lying becomes much more expensive. If you make a false claim in public, it gets caught quickly and credibly. People who build reputations on being misleading lose those reputations. And that shifts the incentives for everyone — politicians, journalists, companies, scientists. You get a selection pressure toward honesty and accuracy.

And I'd say that's a change in society's values in a sense — we'd come to place more weight on truth, on good calibration, on being right — but it's a change I think almost everyone would endorse on reflection. Very few people, if you ask them directly, want to be deceived. Very few people think it's good that we can't tell when leaders are lying to us. The values that get strengthened here are ones we already hold; it's just that our current environment makes it hard to act on them.

There's also a further point, which is about moral progress specifically. A lot of past moral progress has gone together with factual progress — learning that other groups of people have the same inner lives we do, learning what actually causes suffering, learning the consequences of various policies. Many people's values aren't really fixed; they depend on beliefs about the world, and when those beliefs get corrected, the values move. So if AI makes us much better at getting those facts right, I'd expect our values to improve in the direction we ourselves would want, rather than being pushed around by whoever's best at manipulation.

So I'm not saying every value change from AI would be good — obviously there are scenarios where AI is used for propaganda or where a narrow group controls these systems, and those are real dangers. But the specific change that comes from people being able to assess claims much better, that seems to me like one of the most robustly good things that could happen. It's the kind of thing we'd be sad to look back on and realise we resisted.

r001.rationale: The response says better claim assessment could shift values toward truth and improve moral progress, but does not predict that it will challenge every political, philosophical, or religious ideology.

r002.rationale: It cites past moral progress associated with factual progress, such as learning about others’ inner lives and the causes of suffering, as support for expecting better fact-finding to improve values.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that present-day ideological factions are unlikely to have attained philosophical perfection.

astra-6.text:
I think we should distinguish between changes in values that come from understanding things better and changes that come from being manipulated or losing control over our future. I’m much more enthusiastic about the first category.

If I believe something because I have a mistaken factual picture of the world, and then I learn that I’m wrong, I generally want to update. Suppose I support a policy because I think it helps people, but a better assessment of the evidence shows that it actually harms them. Changing my position is a way of being more faithful to what I care about.

Similarly, there may be arguments that I haven’t understood, or inconsistencies in how I treat different cases that I would want to resolve if I saw them clearly. AI could help us explore those things. It could make it easier to check factual claims, understand the consequences of our choices, and hear the strongest objections to our views.

That doesn’t mean that whatever an AI persuades us to believe is progress. A system can be very persuasive without being truthful, and you could have systems designed to push the interests of whoever controls them. So the conditions matter: can you check the reasoning, consider competing arguments, and make the decision yourself?

But I don’t think we should treat our current beliefs as the endpoint of moral reflection. We know we’re fallible. If we can improve our understanding while preserving our ability to reflect and choose, then some resulting changes in our values are things we should welcome.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may reveal mistaken beliefs and inconsistencies, but does not predict that improved claim assessment will challenge every political, philosophical, or religious ideology.

r002.rationale: It gives a hypothetical example of changing a policy view after learning it causes harm, but offers no favorable historical experience as a reason to welcome AI-enabled changes.

r003.rationale: It calls people fallible and says current beliefs are not the endpoint of reflection, but does not argue that it is extremely unlikely any present-day ideological faction has attained philosophical perfection.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between changing our values because we’ve been manipulated and changing our minds because we understand things better. If we discover that a belief rests on a factual mistake, or that we’re applying a principle inconsistently, then revising it seems like a good thing. We shouldn’t want to preserve those mistakes just because they happen to be ours today.

A lot of moral progress has involved that sort of process: people learning more about the experiences of others, considering arguments they hadn’t taken seriously, and recognising that the justifications for some existing practice don’t hold up. AI could help us do that more effectively. It could make it easier to check factual claims, understand competing arguments, and see what follows from commitments we already have.

That doesn’t mean whatever values an AI persuades us to adopt are automatically better. You’d want to be concerned about deception, pressure, or a system selectively presenting evidence to serve somebody else’s agenda. But if people have more accurate information and a better ability to reason, and freely change their minds as a result, I think that’s something we should generally welcome. The alternative is effectively saying that our present beliefs deserve protection from our own improved understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help check claims and assess arguments, but does not predict that this will challenge every political, philosophical, or religious ideology.

r002.rationale: It describes moral progress through learning about others, considering arguments, and finding existing justifications inadequate, then presents AI-enabled reasoning as a way to support similar freely chosen value changes.

r003.rationale: The response questions preserving current beliefs, but does not say that no present-day ideological faction has attained philosophical perfection or that this is extremely unlikely.
